assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 20,000 operations/s: 6,400 messages sent/s expanding to ~12,000 socket deliveries/s (average conversation ~2 online recipients). Group chats change that multiplier directly — a 200-member group is 200 deliveries for one send.

assumptions.subject: lb
assumptions.statement: The load balancer is on the CONNECT and REST paths only, not on every message. A WebSocket is established once and then carries traffic that never crosses the balancer again — which is why its arrival rate is a small fraction of system rps.

assumptions.subject: ws
assumptions.statement: The real sizing constraint for a WebSocket gateway is CONCURRENT CONNECTIONS (memory, file descriptors, TLS session state) — roughly 100k sockets per instance here — not messages per second. The v1 engine has no notion of held connections, so it charges the gateway per FRAME (~5,000/s per instance) and cannot tell you when you run out of sockets. Size for connections separately.

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The message store is HASH-SHARDED by conversation id; 2 shards are modelled as 2 instances, which is the right shape (capacity scales with shards) but assumes an even key distribution. A single hot conversation lands on one shard and the engine will not show that hotspot. Production chat systems use a wide-column store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB) for this; sql_db is the closest kind Keystone models and the throughput figure is set accordingly.

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: Redis holds presence and the socket-routing table (which gateway currently owns which user). Sized for MEMORY and for tail latency, not for rps — hence the low utilisation. On the deliver path it is consulted only when the routing entry is not already local (visit_prob 0.3).

assumptions.subject: delivery
assumptions.statement: Offline delivery, read receipts, typing indicators and push-notification hand-off all ride on the same log in production. Only the online-delivery path is modelled; the push hand-off is a separate system (see the notification blueprint).

assumptions.subject: encryption
assumptions.statement: End-to-end encryption (the reason people name Signal or WhatsApp) changes the SERVER's job, not its throughput shape: the server routes ciphertext it cannot read. Key exchange, device fan-out and sender-key rotation are NOT modelled and add real per-message work.

_library.summary: Persistent WebSocket gateways fan messages out through a durable log to a sharded message store.
